Currency transaction report (CTR): how banks file

MT

Mehak Tariq, CAMSNovember 26, 2026•9 min read

A currency transaction report (CTR) is the report a US bank files with FinCEN for each transaction in currency of more than $10,000, or for several cash transactions it knows are by or for one person when cash in or cash out totals more than $10,000 in one business day. The rule is 31 CFR 1010.311. The bank verifies and records who conducted the transaction, files the CTR electronically within 15 calendar days and keeps a copy for five years. Transactions with exempt persons can be left out; most exempt persons must first be designated.

Below: what counts as reportable, aggregation, identification, filing, exemptions, structuring, and how an operations team runs CTR filing each day. It explains public guidance and is not legal advice.

What a currency transaction report covers

Section 1010.311 requires each financial institution other than a casino to report "each deposit, withdrawal, exchange of currency or other payment or transfer" involving a transaction in currency of more than $10,000. Section 1020.310 points banks to these part 1010 rules.

Currency means coin and paper money. The FFIEC BSA/AML Manual, citing 31 CFR 1010.100(m), defines it as money of the United States or any other country that is legal tender and "customarily used and accepted as a medium of exchange" where it was issued. The manual's list of transactions that can trigger a CTR includes deposits and withdrawals (ATMs included), denomination exchanges, cash loan payments, certificate of deposit purchases, funds transfers and monetary instruments paid for in currency, and certain armored car transactions. A check deposit is not a cash transaction. A single $10,000 transaction with nothing to aggregate needs no CTR, since the rule says "more than $10,000".

Aggregation: one business day, one person

Under section 1010.313, a bank includes all of its domestic branch offices, and multiple cash transactions count as one transaction "if the financial institution has knowledge that they are by or on behalf of any person" and the cash in or cash out totals more than $10,000 during one business day. Deposits made at night, over a weekend or on a holiday are treated as received on the next business day.

FinCEN's CTR FAQs (FAQ 17) set out the arithmetic. Debits are added to debits and credits to credits. If both sides go over $10,000, one CTR can report both, but the bank should not offset cash in against cash out. A deposit to a joint account is presumed to be made on behalf of all account holders (FAQ 23), so each holder is listed in Part I for each role.

Common ownership needs judgment. Citing FinCEN guidance FIN-2012-G001, the FFIEC manual says separately incorporated businesses are presumed independent, so one owner is not by itself a reason to aggregate. Shared staff and address, or one company's account repeatedly paying another's expenses or the owner's personal bills, may show they are not run independently.

Identification the CTR needs

Section 1010.312 requires the bank, before it concludes a reportable transaction, to verify and record the name and address of the individual presenting it. It must also record the identity, account number and Social Security or taxpayer identification number, if any, of anyone on whose behalf the transaction is made.

  • For a non-resident or someone who says they are an alien, verification is by passport, alien identification card or other official document showing nationality or residence.
  • For everyone else, it is a document other than a signature card that banks normally accept when cashing checks for non-depositors, such as a driver's license.
  • The specific identifying details, such as the license number, go on the report. A mere notation of "known customer" or "bank signature card on file" is prohibited.

The checks resemble KYC verification, applied at the window to whoever is physically present, who may not be the account holder.

Completing and filing the CTR

All CTRs go through FinCEN's BSA E-Filing System. A CTR is due within 15 days of the transaction under section 1010.306(a)(1), and FinCEN's FAQ 12 confirms that since April 1, 2013 "all FinCEN CTRs must be filed within 15 calendar days of the reported transaction(s)." The bank keeps a copy for five years from the date of the report (section 1010.306(a)(2)), on paper or electronically.

From FinCEN's FAQs:

  • Critical fields, marked with an asterisk, need either the information or the "Unknown" box checked. For other fields, FinCEN expects "the most complete filing information available".
  • Each person gets a Part I for each role they played: conducting on their own behalf, conducting for another, or having it conducted for them (FAQs 16 and 22).
  • BSA E-Filing does not keep records, so the bank saves its own copy before submitting (FAQs 8 and 9).
  • Accepted filings are acknowledged within 48 hours with a BSA ID (FAQ 14). An amendment checks "Correct/amend prior report" and gives the earlier BSA ID (FAQ 6).

A bank that finds missed or wrong CTRs must begin complying. The FFIEC manual says that in most cases it can file late or amended CTRs without asking FinCEN first, and should consider contacting FinCEN when its regulator says so or when it is unclear whether backfiling is required.

CTR exemptions

Section 1020.315 lets a bank skip CTRs for transactions with exempt persons. Exempt persons are banks (domestic operations), government agencies and bodies exercising governmental authority, companies listed on the NYSE, American Stock Exchange or NASDAQ (with exclusions), subsidiaries at least 51 percent owned by a listed company, non-listed businesses and payroll customers.

For non-listed businesses and payroll customers, the customer must generally have had a transaction account for two months (a documented risk-based assessment can shorten this), be organized or registered in the United States, and "frequently" transact more than $10,000 in cash. FinCEN guidance FIN-2012-G003 says that means at least five reportable transactions within a year. Some businesses are ineligible, among them financial institutions, vehicle dealers, law, accounting and medical practices, pawnbrokers and real estate brokers. A business with mixed activities can qualify if no more than 50 percent of its gross revenue comes from ineligible ones.

The process rules:

  • The bank designates the customer on FinCEN Form 110 within 30 calendar days after the first reportable transaction it wants to exempt. No designation is needed for Federal Reserve Banks, other banks or government bodies.
  • At least once a year, the bank reviews whether each listed company, subsidiary, non-listed business and payroll customer is still eligible.
  • A transaction an exempt person conducts as an agent for the real owner of the funds is not exempt.
  • The exemption never removes the duty to report suspicious activity. The rule's own example is "a sharp increase from one year to the next" in an exempt customer's cash.

The FFIEC manual's section on exempt persons calls the first five categories Phase I and the last two Phase II. A bank that exempted accounts improperly must start filing CTRs and can revoke the exemption on a DOEP report marked "Exemption Revoked".

Structuring and the CTR threshold

Structuring is breaking up cash to avoid a CTR. Section 1010.314 prohibits anyone, to evade the reporting rules, from causing a bank to skip a CTR or file one with a material omission or misstatement, or from structuring transactions. The definition in 31 CFR 1010.100(xx) covers transactions "in any amount, at one or more financial institutions, on one or more days, in any manner". FinCEN's customer notice gives examples, such as $15,000 split between two tellers in one day.

FinCEN's October 2025 SAR FAQs say cash at or near $10,000 is not, by itself, enough to require a suspicious activity report. A SAR is required only if the bank "knows, suspects, or has reason to suspect" the activity is designed to evade CTR reporting, and the SAR rule applies at $5,000 or more. The AML program should still be designed to detect and report structuring, with monitoring matched to the bank's risk. The evidence and decision on each alert belong in the case file, covered in our guides to AML case management and writing a SAR narrative. Transaction monitoring alert triage shows how those alerts reach an analyst.

How a bank operations team runs CTR filing

A daily routine for the CTR report:

  1. Pull the business day's cash activity from every branch, ATM, night drop and armored car feed, moving night and weekend deposits to the next business day.
  2. Aggregate by person. Add cash in and cash out separately for each conductor and each person on whose behalf cash moved, including joint account holders and businesses you have decided to treat as one person.
  3. List every total over $10,000. Check each against the exemption list: is a Form 110 on file where one is required, is the account an exemptible account, and was the customer acting for someone else?
  4. Check the identification captured. If the license number or taxpayer ID is missing, get it and fix the teller step that missed it.
  5. Prepare the CTR: one Part I per person per role, specific occupations, every critical field filled or marked unknown.
  6. Have someone other than the preparer approve the filing. The FFIEC manual says "employees who complete CTRs generally should not also be responsible for the decision to file the reports". It also lists BSA officer or senior approval for staff overrides of aggregation systems as a control.
  7. File through BSA E-Filing well inside 15 calendar days, save the copy, and match each submission to its acknowledgement and BSA ID.
  8. Send any pattern that looks like structuring to the AML alert queue. Totals over $10,000 still get a CTR; whether to file a SAR is a separate decision.
  9. Once a year, run the exemption review and check how the monitoring system covers each non-listed business and payroll customer account.

Common questions

What is a CTR in banking?

It is the FinCEN report a bank files when cash in or cash out by or for one person on one business day totals more than $10,000. FinCEN's customer notice says "There is no general prohibition against handling large amounts of currency", and the CTR is required whatever the reason for the cash.

Does a CTR apply to checks or wires?

Only when currency is involved. Buying a wire or a cashier's check with more than $10,000 in cash is reportable; depositing a check is not.

Can a bank stop filing CTRs for a busy cash business?

Yes, if it qualifies as a non-listed business, the bank files Form 110 in time and reviews it every year. Monitoring and suspicious activity reporting still apply.
